title: Cumulative learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity

concept.text: The innovation would let a general-purpose model accumulate useful competence through successive rounds of learning while preserving both earlier abilities and its capacity to acquire new ones. A model could encounter changing domains, update its learned representations, and continue benefiting from its history without requiring full replay of its original pretraining corpus. Achieving this jointly at general-purpose model scale remains the target described here.

Two distinct failures define the problem. Catastrophic forgetting degrades previously acquired competence as learning proceeds. Loss of plasticity degrades the ability to learn new information, potentially leaving an experienced network learning or generalizing less effectively than a freshly initialized comparator. A cumulative learner needs stability for useful prior knowledge and plasticity for subsequent learning. Preserving either capability alone leaves the joint objective incomplete.

significance.text: Dohare and colleagues' 2024 Nature paper describes a common practical pattern in which learning is turned off during deployment and substantial new data is incorporated by training a replacement network on old and new data together. Reliable cumulative learning could let organizations carry forward a model's acquired competence through successive updates and reduce reliance on repeated full retraining. The paper's accompanying author response also clarifies that its deployment description concerns typical practice, leaving room for systems that already continue learning.

Conditional synthesis. If retention and plasticity remained reliable over long deployment histories, models could accumulate expertise as their environments and users' needs changed. The revolutionary consequence would be continuity of learned competence across updates, with earlier learning supporting an evolving system. Reduced retraining cost, faster adaptation and positive transfer are additional possibilities whose realization would depend on the method's compute, memory, replay and learning-speed requirements.

Impact limits. A successful finite benchmark would establish cumulative learning over its tested distributions, duration and resource limits. Years of unrestricted learning, lower total computation and resolution of every stability–plasticity tradeoff would require further evidence. One-shot acquisition of personal facts, counterfactual reasoning, causal planning and learning from scarce irreversible outcomes each involve additional capabilities beyond the retention-and-plasticity objective.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a scalable learning method that maintains useful prior competence while remaining effective at acquiring new competence through a long, changing sequence of domains. The supplied studies motivate this joint objective and document failures of existing approaches in particular settings. Their findings leave open which combinations of learning rules, representations and resource policies can sustain both requirements at general-purpose model scale without full original-corpus replay.

An engineering barrier is coordinating preservation and renewal within a network. Updating parameters can damage earlier abilities, while preserving an experienced network's parameters and structure does not by itself guarantee continued adaptability. Continual backpropagation demonstrates that selectively reinitializing low-utility units can preserve plasticity in studied settings. Its authors explicitly leave forgetting untreated, so a complete solution must also show how prior competence survives the updates and representational changes needed for new learning.

Joudaki and colleagues analyze mechanisms that can trap learning dynamics in states associated with plasticity loss. Their theoretical trapping results depend on stated architectural and dynamical conditions, including invariance results for particular affine manifolds under gradient flow and gradient-descent dynamics. Open questions include nonlinear manifolds, stability, and the extent to which interventions can restore fresh-model exploration and generalization. These conditional results leave the broad possibilities of gradient-based cumulative learning unresolved.

Engineering synthesis. A practical demonstration must make its resource policy explicit. Replay allowance, stored examples, parameter growth, update computation and learning speed can materially change what has been achieved. A method that succeeds through expanding memory or capacity can still provide evidence of cumulative learning, with the demonstrated capability bounded by those costs. Evaluation must also distinguish declining plasticity from increasing task difficulty and track intermediate failures that an endpoint measurement could conceal.

current_state.text: Dohare and colleagues' Nature paper, published on 21 August 2024 in volume 632, pages 768–774, documents plasticity loss in studied vision and reinforcement-learning settings. Its text reports that standard deep-learning methods eventually learned no better than shallow networks in the relevant experiments. In representative Continual ImageNet experiments, networks initially achieved up to 88 percent test accuracy on early tasks and had lost substantial plasticity by task 2,000 across the tested step-size values. The early-task accuracy describes performance when those tasks were encountered and supplies no corresponding measurement of their later retention.

Continual backpropagation selectively reinitialized low-utility units and maintained plasticity over the tested horizons. The reinforcement-learning results combined the method with L2 regularization. These experiments show that interventions can mitigate plasticity loss within the tested architectures and settings. The authors explicitly state that their method does not tackle forgetting, leaving simultaneous retention and continued plasticity at language-model scale un demonstrated by these results.

The Nature paper also described its extensive systematic study as prohibitively expensive to perform with large language models at the time of publication. That feasibility assessment belongs to its 2024 context. The supplied review found that the forgetting distinction, practical retraining discussion, numerical results and language-model feasibility statement appear in different locations in the paper. The retained HTML and PDF extractions were partial, with the PDF text truncated at page 17, so the account here relies on the passages identified in the supplied review.

Joudaki and colleagues' preprint, Barriers for Learning in an Evolving World, was submitted on 30 September 2025 and revised on 17 May 2026. The reviewed version analyzes plasticity-loss mechanisms and demonstrates mitigation and recovery in selected settings. Its conclusion leaves substantive questions about nonlinear manifolds, stability, and restoration of exploration and generalization open. The supplied record establishes its arXiv preprint status. The PDF extraction skipped some form content after exceeding an extraction limit, and the figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review.

The research notes also cite an ACM Computing Surveys article through DOI 10.1145/3735633, assign it a publication date of 20 November 2025, and attribute to it a statement about degradation of prior knowledge in pretrained language models. No retained source artifact was available for that citation in the supplied review. Its bibliographic details and attributed statement therefore remain unverified within this record.

Evidence-coverage limitation. The supplied materials document dated findings and continuing work through the May 2026 preprint revision. Their freshness record is empty, so they do not establish comprehensive coverage of the field through 1 November 2026. They contain no demonstrated completion of the joint general-purpose-scale capability defined here.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Begin with a model that matches a published general-purpose baseline on a frozen evaluation suite. Continue training it through a pre-registered, long sequence of new domains without full replay of the original pretraining corpus. Specify model scale, sequence length, domain order, access to task boundaries, replay allowance, memory use, capacity growth and training budgets before interpreting the outcome. These are proposed operational criteria for this record.
completion_criteria.label: Baseline-matching model completes long domain sequence without full pretraining replay

completion_criteria.text: Proposed retention test. Reevaluate the original frozen suite and previously encountered domains throughout the sequence, including early, intermediate and final checkpoints. Require performance to remain within pre-registered degradation tolerances, with uncertainty reported. The proposal permits bounded degradation. Measurements should reveal whether apparent overall retention conceals severe losses in particular domains or abilities.
completion_criteria.label: Earlier abilities remain within preregistered degradation tolerances throughout learning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed plasticity test. At multiple stages, compare acquisition of new domains with freshly initialized models trained on the corresponding domains under matched data and training budgets. Pre-register the statistical tolerance for matching their performance and report learning curves and generalization. The final new domain should meet the same criterion. Fresh-training comparisons have a precedent in the Nature paper's effort to distinguish plasticity loss from differences in task difficulty, although the exact comparator proposed here is an evaluation choice.
completion_criteria.label: New-domain acquisition matches fresh training through the final domain

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical-boundary test. Demonstrate retention and continued learning together across repeated runs, multiple domain orders and independently reproducible implementations or adequately specified artifacts. Report replay storage, total computation, update latency, capacity growth and learning speed alongside competence. Test further shifts and longer horizons to map where performance degrades. Any successful finite program establishes demonstrated breadth within those conditions, with further claims requiring additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible retention and plasticity with reported resource costs and limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. MLC-01, A predictive theory of what deep networks learn, could help explain when updates preserve prior representations or damage them. Its central objective is predictive understanding of learning. MLC-03 concerns sustained cumulative competence, which could be demonstrated empirically even while such a theory remained incomplete.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-02, Domain learning at a human experience budget, overlaps through efficient acquisition of new competence. MLC-03 additionally requires retention and continuing adaptability across successive learning episodes. A cumulative learner could still require large amounts of experience, while efficient learning of one domain could coexist with later forgetting or plasticity loss.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-04, World models that survive novel interventions, concerns robustness of learned world models under interventions. Cumulative learning could preserve and update such models, while intervention robustness requires separate evaluation. The supplied roster gives no detailed specification establishing a dependency between MLC-04 and MLC-03, or making MLC-04 a prerequisite for one-shot factual acquisition.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-05, Local credit assignment that matches backpropagation at scale, concerns how learning signals produce effective updates. Such a mechanism could contribute to a cumulative learner, but its equivalence to backpropagation would leave retention and long-term plasticity as separate requirements. MLC-06, Algorithmic legibility sufficient to verify and edit a model, could support diagnosis and targeted modification of learned competence. Legibility and editable behavior would each need their own demonstrations alongside cumulative learning.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-07, Open-ended curricula that create externally verified new competencies, concerns generating learning opportunities and validating resulting abilities. MLC-03 concerns retaining competence and remaining able to learn as those opportunities accumulate. MLC-08, Discovery of new empirical laws, confirmed by experiment, could benefit from an accumulating scientific learner, while independently requiring experimentally confirmed discovery.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-09, Skill learning from scarce, irreversible, real-world outcomes, shares an interest in adaptation over experience and adds constraints on feedback scarcity and the consequences of actions. Preserving plasticity alone leaves those constraints unresolved. The roster title supports this distinction, while the earlier claim of a specific dependency involving MLC-09 exceeds the supplied detail.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-10, Non-vacuous behavioral certificates at frontier scale, concerns meaningful assurance about behavior. Repeated retention and learning tests provide empirical evidence within their coverage, while certificates require their own defined guarantees. MLC-11, Frontier competence at a biological-order power budget, overlaps through resource efficiency. A cumulative learner's energy use must be measured independently of its retention and plasticity.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish simultaneous retention and continued plasticity at general-purpose language-model scale under an explicit original-corpus replay restriction.
Sequence length, model scale, retention tolerances, statistical matching criteria and acceptable resource costs remain choices for a concrete experimental protocol.
The ACM survey's bibliographic details and attributed statement remain unverified because no source artifact was retained.
The Nature extractions are partial. The Joudaki PDF extraction omitted some form content, and its figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review.
The empty freshness record leaves comprehensive field coverage through 1 November 2026 unresolved.
The detailed specifications of MLC-04 and MLC-09 are absent, leaving the originally asserted dependencies unverified.
The extent of recoverable plasticity, including restoration of fresh-model exploration and generalization under broader conditions, remains open in the reviewed preprint.

brief.title: AI that keeps learning without losing earlier skills
possible: You could keep using an AI model as your needs changed, letting it learn new subjects while preserving earlier skills. It would also retain its ability to learn, so a long learning history would not leave it struggling to acquire the next skill.
The model could build on successive updates without having to study its entire original training collection again.
why: Organizations could carry a model’s accumulated expertise forward instead of repeatedly training replacements on old and new material. Earlier learning could remain useful as the model’s work changed.
This could reduce repeated retraining and help models adapt faster, allowing experience to support future learning.

sources.showed: In image recognition and learning through rewards, standard methods gradually lost their ability to learn. Resetting less-used parts of the network preserved that ability over the tested sequences.
sources.quote: Here we show that they do not—that standard deep-learning methods gradually lose plasticity in continual-learning settings until they learn no better than a shallow network.
sources.cited_for: Models can lose their ability to learn, and targeted resets can help preserve it.
sources.not_established: The method does not address forgetting or demonstrate both abilities together in a general-purpose language model.

sources.showed: This is a survey discussing degradation of earlier knowledge in language models that have already been trained.
sources.cited_for: Earlier knowledge can degrade during further learning in language models.
sources.not_established: A survey does not demonstrate a model that preserves earlier skills while continuing to learn.

sources.who: Amir Joudaki and colleagues at ETH Zürich and Apple
sources.showed: They identified mathematical traps that can prevent further learning under specified conditions. Experiments showed that changes to network structure could restore learning ability in selected settings.
sources.quote: We identify two primary mechanisms that create these traps: frozen units from activation saturation and cloned-unit manifolds from representational redundancy.
sources.cited_for: Learning can become trapped, and some interventions can restore the ability to learn.
sources.not_established: The results do not establish broad recovery of learning ability together with preservation of earlier skills.

shown: Dohare and colleagues preserved plasticity—the ability to learn new information—by repeatedly resetting less-used parts of a network. Their experiments covered image recognition and learning through rewards, but the method did not tackle forgetting.

Joudaki and colleagues explained some ways networks become trapped and demonstrated recovery in selected settings. Neither study demonstrated a general-purpose model that both retains earlier skills and keeps learning across a long sequence of changing subjects.
missing: A general-purpose model must preserve earlier skills and keep acquiring new ones through a long sequence without replaying all its original training data.
Repeated tests must track both abilities throughout learning, so temporary or subject-specific failures remain visible.
Success must come with explicit costs for stored examples, computation, model growth and learning speed.

milestones.label: A capable model completes a long learning sequence
milestones.explanation: A model matching a published general-purpose baseline would complete a long, predefined sequence of new subjects without replaying all its original training data. This establishes the setting for testing cumulative learning.

milestones.label: Earlier skills survive throughout learning
milestones.explanation: Earlier skills would stay within predefined limits on performance loss at checkpoints throughout the sequence. This would establish that continued learning preserves useful prior competence.

milestones.label: New learning keeps pace with fresh models
milestones.explanation: The experienced model would match fresh models on new subjects under equal data and training budgets, including the final subject. This would establish that its ability to learn persists.

milestones.label: Both abilities repeat with clear costs and limits
milestones.explanation: Independent implementations and repeated runs with different subject orders would reproduce both abilities, report resource costs and test longer sequences. This would establish reliability and reveal where success ends.

uncertain: How long must learning continue, and how much loss of earlier skills is acceptable?
Can restored learning ability also recover performance on unfamiliar examples, rather than merely fit new training data?
Which memory, computation and model-growth costs would make cumulative learning practical?

page.title: Continual learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity
page.definition: A pretrained model used across domains accumulates abilities through successive updates without replaying its full original training corpus. It retains earlier abilities and plasticity—the capacity to acquire new abilities—as learning continues.

goal.need: In Dohare et al.'s Continual ImageNet experiments, networks reached up to 88% accuracy on early binary tasks but lost plasticity by task 2,000 at every tested learning rate. Continual backpropagation sustained new-task learning over 5,000 tasks; plotted results averaged 30 runs. Its authors explicitly leave forgetting untreated. DARPA's Lifelong Learning Machines programme seeks adaptation without forgetting previous learning.

statements.quote: seeks to develop fundamentally new ML approaches that allow systems to adapt continually to new circumstances without forgetting previous learning.
continual learning, the ability for a model to actively acquire new knowledge and skills over time without forgetting old ones.
statements.context: The passage identifies a remaining challenge for large language models.

completion.title: Independent experiments show a general-purpose model retains old skills and preserves new-task learning.
completion.criterion: A general-purpose pretrained model passes the same finite task-stream experiment in an original study and an independent reproduction. Starting-ability scores never fall below their pre-update values; acquired-task scores never fall below their immediate post-learning values. Each later task matches or exceeds a copy started from the original pretrained checkpoint, using no more task examples under matched update budgets. These conditions hold at every evaluation. Model capacity and replay storage have fixed bounds; the full original pretraining corpus is unavailable. Achievement is restricted to the tested stream and budgets.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body located that defines this joint general-purpose-model test.
completion.basis: Searches covered DARPA L2M goals and evaluation thresholds, NIST and ISO materials, developer statements, and continual-learning benchmark and prize criteria. No joint pass test specifying a horizon, tolerances and replay limits for general-purpose pretrained models was found. This fallback combines taskwise retention, acquisition against the original pretrained starting point and independent reproduction. DARPA's published aggregate thresholds supply component tests, not this completion standard.

milestones.title: A continual learner retains earlier performance with a performance-maintenance score of at least zero.
milestones.criterion: Performance Maintenance (PM) ≥ 0 in the published L2M evaluation: mean later performance on learned tasks is no lower than initially. Baker et al. report 3 of 18 configurations meeting this boundary. Averaging can conceal individual task losses.
milestones.set_by: DARPA L2M evaluation teams; Baker et al., Section 4.2.2.
milestones.threshold_quote: The LL threshold value for PM is zero

milestones.title: A continual learner reaches PM ≥ 0 and FT, BT, RP and SE ≥ 1 in the same environment.
milestones.criterion: Meet PM ≥ 0 and FT, BT, RP and SE ≥ 1 together. These denote performance maintenance, forward/backward transfer, performance relative to single-task experts and sample efficiency. Baker et al. report Teledyne's AirSim agent meeting these boundaries, scoring 0.56±0.98, 11.69±0.47, 1.00±0.01, 1.03±0.04 and 2.74±1.70, respectively (mean±standard deviation). Aggregate success does not establish taskwise retention or unlimited plasticity.
milestones.set_by: DARPA L2M evaluation teams; Baker et al., Section 4, Tables 3–5.
milestones.threshold_quote: any interference, forgetting, or performance not equal to or better than an STE

milestones.title: One general-purpose model shows taskwise retention and undiminished acquisition on a finite task stream.
milestones.criterion: One experiment meets the completion test's taskwise retention and fresh-copy acquisition conditions, with bounded capacity and replay storage and no full original-corpus replay, before independent reproduction. Tiwari et al.'s preprint revised on 14 October 2026 reports Qwen3-8B adaptation over three tasks, 200 updates each. Its six-task Qwen3-4B experiment uses 3,200 training and 200 held-out problems per task, but evaluates only the current task. These results do not establish passage of the joint test; peer review is not established in the cited record.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback for a single experimental demonstration of the joint completion conditions.

not_found: No independent reproduction satisfying the joint general-purpose-model test was located.
The number of independent AirSim runs underlying Baker et al.'s Table 8 was not found.

results.finding: CIFAR-100 base system, 30 runs: incremental accuracy was 5% lower than retraining at 100 classes.
results.detail: The experiment bears on plasticity but used a task-specific image classifier, not a general-purpose pretrained model. It trained on all available old classes and did not test taskwise retention against immediate post-learning scores.
results.quote: By the end, when all 100 classes were available, the accuracy of the incrementally trained base system was 5% lower than the retrained network (a performance drop equivalent to that of removing a notable algorithmic advance, such as batch normalization).

results.finding: MLP, CNN, ResNet and ViT models showed declining training accuracy across 40 sequential Tiny ImageNet tasks.
results.detail: The experiment addresses acquisition during continual learning, but does not establish taskwise retention or comparison with copies of an original pretrained checkpoint.
results.quote:
The
plots illustrate (across different architectures like MLP, CNN, ResNet, and ViT from left to right)
an increase in the fraction of dead or duplicate units during training, coincidental with a decrease in
training accuracy.

results.finding: Teledyne UML agent, one configuration: mean PM was 0.56.
results.detail: The AirSim evaluation used permutations of classification task variants. The number of runs is not stated. Mean PM can conceal losses on individual tasks.

results.finding: Teledyne’s AirSim UML agent met 5 of 5 metric thresholds across runs; sample size not stated.
results.detail: Mean±SD: PM 0.56±0.98, FT 11.69±0.47, BT 1.00±0.01, RP 1.03±0.04, and SE 2.74±1.70. Results are aggregates across task-variant orderings; they do not establish taskwise retention or unlimited plasticity.

results.finding: Learner 1.0: nine of ten skills retained within two correct answers on 225 held-out questions per skill.
results.detail: The fixed-capacity model learned ten skills sequentially without replay. Oriel fell from 12 to 9 correct. The source reports no fresh-copy acquisition comparison, so it does not establish the joint test.
results.quote: Nine of the ten finish within two correct answers of their own-end score on fixed 225-question panels, after a stream of 63,282 updates.
